b: PPC Land is now also on WhatsApp, with a new PPC Land channel carrying its stories.

A PPC Land special edition on Amazon's advertising business, published November 14, 2026. It covers the period from Amazon's first public hints about advertising revenue in 2017 to Amazon Ads Support Center changes dated November 13, 2026, with most of the detail drawn from the years since the pandemic began in March 2020. Revenue figures come from Amazon's filings and earnings releases as reported in the linked coverage. Growth rates are given as each source reported them; where Landline has calculated a figure itself, the text says so.

On Friday morning, November 14, 2026, PPC Land published an account of a help page that most advertisers will never read. Amazon's Support Center guide to building a DVA+ campaign, updated the previous day, now limits each automated campaign to 20 products, offers three routes into the product with the automated one selected by default, and lists seven possible campaign objectives while showing each advertiser only those it is eligible for. It advises against budget caps on the grounds that they can cause under-delivery, warns that changing a key performance indicator after launch resets what the system has learned, and leaves audio, a format Amazon has sold programmatically for years, out of the default flow altogether. Two days earlier, another Support Center change had told agencies that the campaign-level fee setting they have used inside Amazon's demand-side platform can be set only until January 31, 2027, after which agency fees move into manager accounts that Amazon controls and describes, in its own words, with the line "Amazon doesn't bill agency fees." None of this was announced on a stage. It is the plumbing of an advertising business that took in $78.0 billion over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, and it shows where that business is now heading: from selling inventory to the people who plan media, towards deciding, by default, how the media is planned.

The Landline newsletter can also be heard. Marketing Is Calling reads each edition aloud every day, on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube. Marketing Rodeo picks the most controversial advertising story of each day, weekends included, and has some fun with it, on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube.

The DVA+ guide is a useful place to start because it is so ordinary. DVA is the name Amazon gave its demand-side platform at the unBoxed conference in San Francisco on September 29, 2026, when it retired the Amazon DSP brand and folded the buying tool and its advertising console into a conversational interface called Amazon Ads Agent. The letters stand for display, video and audio. DVA+ is the simplified, automated mode of that product, and since September it has been the default way into it. The guide PPC Land described on November 14 sets out what that default now means in practice.

There are three ways to build a campaign. The first, labelled DVA+, is pre-selected. The second, DVA+ advanced, exposes more controls. The third, a legacy mode, preserves the older demand-side platform workflow for buyers who still want it. In the default route, an advertiser picks an objective from the list the system offers, adds up to 20 products, accepts or edits AI-generated creative and sets a budget, which can be monthly, daily or lifetime. Three objectives apply to Amazon's own properties: sales on Amazon, optimised to total return on ad spend; traffic on Amazon, measured by cost per detail page view, which the guide says is reported but not optimised to; and awareness on Amazon, described as reach "at optimal frequency". Display, online video and streaming television are the default formats. Location targeting is available only for objectives that point off Amazon. Up to three frequency caps can be set for each ad group, at user or household level. Managed-service clients pay a fee calculated as a percentage and invoiced separately. And pressing the launch button does not, by itself, start a campaign.

Each of these choices can be defended on its own terms. A cap of 20 products keeps the creative system from trying to promote a whole catalogue at once. Hiding objectives an advertiser cannot use reduces errors. The warning on budget caps, that they "can cause under-delivery by blocking full budget use", is technically true of almost any automated buying system. But taken together, and set beside the rest of what Amazon changed in the same week, they describe a product designed around the assumption that the machine sets the parameters and the human approves them. PPC Land listed what the guide leaves out: no default value for the frequency caps, no percentage for the managed-service fee, no explanation of what "reach at optimal frequency" means, no rule for how product variations count towards the limit of 20, and no statement of which countries or beta stage the page applies to. It also noted that the guide gives two different sets of launch instructions.

That last point matters more than it sounds. On October 29, PPC Land reported that the conversational Ads Agent experience is still in closed beta in 25 countries, that DVA+ advanced settings are limited to some US advertisers, and that Amazon's own pages disagree on which markets keep the old DSP experience, with one list naming 21 countries. Advertisers with programmatic experience get both tiers. New advertisers and those coming from Sponsored Ads get DVA+ only, and must ask an account manager if they want the advanced controls. Agencies with existing entity access get both. DVA+ is billed on a cost-per-thousand basis with no minimum spend, and payment is by invoice only, with credit cards promised for the first quarter of 2027. Destaney Wishon, chief executive of the agency btr media, captured the confusion on LinkedIn with a line PPC Land quoted: "DSP is no longer DSP. It is DVA." She went on to suggest that advertisers who do not own their seat on the platform should move to own it sooner rather than later, which is the kind of advice agencies give when they suspect the ground under their contracts is shifting.
The agency fee moves to the manager account

The second Support Center change, dated November 11 and reported by PPC Land at 21:31 UTC on November 12, is narrower and more revealing. Agencies buying through Amazon's platform have long been able to set a fee on each campaign, so that the client's invoice reflects the agency's margin. That legacy setting can be applied until January 31, 2027 and will be removed entirely by the end of March 2027. Campaigns that keep it will not receive new features. In its place, Amazon has put agency fees for display, video and audio into open beta inside manager accounts, in all marketplaces.

The new structure is more elaborate than the old one. There are five ways to calculate a fee: four markups, based on supply cost alone, supply cost plus the Amazon audience fee, supply cost plus the total audience fee, and supply cost plus the total audience fee plus third-party pre-bid charges, and one margin, calculated as a percentage of budget. A fee can be applied to all current and future accounts, to specific accounts, to specific campaigns or to specific ad groups, and when more than one could apply, "the most specific fee is used". Amazon's worked example takes a 3.5% markup on $10,000 of supply cost and produces a $350 fee and a $10,350 total. Its percentage-of-budget formula, applied to the same figures, gives $362.69, which PPC Land calculated as 3.63% of $10,000, and which cannot be squared with the sentence that follows it on the same page. Two further lines define the relationship. "Amazon doesn't bill agency fees," the page says, and "Advertiser accounts can't set agency fees."

Neither sentence is hostile. The first means the agency invoices its client separately; the second means a brand cannot impose or remove its agency's margin from inside its own account. But the arrangement places the fee in a layer of Amazon's software that Amazon designs, and PPC Land listed the questions the page does not answer: whether clients can see the agency fees column, whether the fees apply to DVA+ campaigns at all, what happens to legacy fees on campaigns already running, and whether a change made in mid-flight applies to the whole campaign. If agency fees do not reach the automated tier that Amazon has made the default, then the default is also the one route on which the agency's margin is invisible to Amazon's billing.

The same evening, PPC Land published three more accounts of Support Center pages updated on November 11. One found that Amazon's 16 benchmark recommendations never suggest cutting budgets: the page sets out eight metrics, each with a favourable and an unfavourable set of actions, and where cost per click or cost per thousand impressions sits below the benchmark, the advice is to "test increasing bids". Another reported that advertisers will lose unmigrated reports on January 31, 2027, with the old report pages going read-only on December 17 and ten report types, including pricing transparency, conversion path and Amazon Attribution reports, unable to migrate yet. A third counted the dimensions in the replacement system and found that 85 of Amazon's 156 unified report dimensions apply to Sponsored Products, against 137 that carry the DVA+ marker, with 59 that apply to DVA+ alone.

Read separately, these are housekeeping. Read together, they describe a platform consolidating the places where an outside party used to add value: the choice of products and objectives, the selection of deals, the setting of budgets, the invoicing of margin and the export of history. That is the argument of this special edition. Amazon spent the years after 2018 building the inventory, the data and the cheapest demand-side platform in the market, in large part to win budgets that agencies controlled. It is now in a second phase, in which the money already flowing through its systems is spent inside defaults Amazon writes. The rest of this piece sets out how it got here, with the numbers, the dates and the evidence on both sides.

Amazon did not publish an advertising revenue figure of its own until February 3, 2022. Before then, the money sat inside a line called "other", which the company described in its filings as sales not otherwise included elsewhere, "such as certain advertising services and our co-branded credit card agreements". Executives said on most earnings calls that advertising made up the bulk of it, and analysts treated the line as a proxy. The table below follows that convention for 2016 to 2020 and switches to the advertising services line Amazon has reported since. The two series are close but not identical, and the break is marked.

Changes and shares are Landline calculations from the figures shown.

Three things stand out. The first is the scale of the compounding. On the figures above, the line Amazon used to call "other" was worth less than $3 billion in 2016; the advertising business that replaced it took in more than $78 billion in the twelve months to the end of September 2026, roughly 26 times as much. Over the same stretch, Amazon's total quarterly sales for the four quarters to September 2026 added up to about $797 billion on Landline's arithmetic, a little under six times the 2016 total. Advertising, in other words, has grown several times faster than the company around it, and its share of Amazon's sales has risen from about 2% to nearly 10%.

The second is that the growth did not come in a straight line. The leap in 2018 was flattered by an accounting change: Digiday reported in April 2018 that Amazon had moved some advertising revenue into the "other" line from January that year, adding $560 million in the first quarter alone. The pandemic years then produced the steepest real acceleration, before growth settled at around 20% a year between 2022 and 2025, a rate that would be remarkable for almost any other advertising business of that size. In 2026 the quarterly pattern has been distorted by a calendar change, of which more below.

The third is that advertising has become one of the main sources of Amazon's profit, even though the company does not say how much it earns from it. Amazon reports operating income for its North America, International and Amazon Web Services segments, and advertising is spread across the first two. Brian Olsavsky, the chief financial officer, told analysts in February 2022 that advertising "only works if we make it useful for customers", and CNBC noted that Amazon had never disclosed advertising operating income. It still has not. The margin on a sponsored product placement sold against Amazon's own search results, with no content to license and no publisher to pay, is widely assumed to be far higher than that on retail, but that assumption rests on inference rather than disclosure.
The years the number sat in "other"

The first public sign that Amazon's advertising business had become material came in October 2017. Search Engine Land estimated after Amazon's third-quarter results that advertising revenue had passed $1 billion in the quarter, roughly double the level of early 2016, on the reasoning that the "other" line was "basically advertising". Olsavsky said on the call that "advertising revenue continues to grow very quickly", and that its growth was faster than the line it sat in. Three months later, MarTech reported that "other" had grown 60% to $1.7 billion in the fourth quarter of 2017, within total revenue of $60.5 billion. Dave Fildes, then director of investor relations, said that "advertising was also a key contributor".

By April 2018 the line had reached $2 billion a quarter. Digiday's account of the first-quarter results ran under the headline "Amazon advertising is now worth $2 billion", and quoted Olsavsky's description of advertising as "a multibillion program". Marketing Dive, summarising the same results on April 30, 2018, noted that Amazon did not specifically break down its advertising revenue, and cited a ClickZ and GroupM study in which 63% of brands planned to increase their Amazon budgets, against 54% for Google and 53% for Facebook. Merkle data in the Digiday piece put the year-on-year rise in Sponsored Products cost per click at 65%. Even then, the price of an Amazon click was rising faster than the volume of clicks.

The same year brought the first reorganisation of the product line. On September 5, 2018, AdExchanger reported that the Amazon Advertising Platform had become Amazon DSP, and that Amazon Media Group and Amazon Marketing Services had been retired under a single Amazon Advertising name. Digiday's cheat sheet the following day noted that Headline Search Ads had become Sponsored Brands and that Amazon's quarterly advertising revenue had reached $2.2 billion, up 129%. GeekWire's account of the full year put "other" revenue at $10.1 billion in 2018, with $3.4 billion in the fourth quarter alone, up 95%, while reminding readers that Amazon did "not break out specific financials for advertising". In 2019 the line reached roughly $14.1 billion, up 39%, and Fildes offered the explanation that would become Amazon's standard pitch: "We're uniquely positioned to do this given our retail business."

The pitch was not only to brands. In July 2018, Digiday reported that Amazon's advertising sales team was increasingly meeting marketers and chief marketing officers directly, cutting agencies out of conversations they had once led. Seth Dallaire, then vice president of worldwide advertising sales, described Amazon's offer to brands as helping them "put together a promotional plan to help make it successful". Dan Salzman, global head of media at HP, which then ranked Amazon as its third-biggest media partner behind Facebook and Google, said that "the benefits of working directly with Amazon are greater speed and operational efficiency". Amazon told Digiday that agencies remained important, and Marketing Dive's summary the next day recorded the same assurance. Kevin Packler of the Knoxville agency Tombras Group described Amazon as "neither a pure-play competitor nor a pure-play ad platform. It's in the middle." Eight years later, that middle position is the one Amazon is now trying to leave.

Amazon finally broke the number out on February 3, 2022. AdExchanger's headline was "Amazon Breaks Out Advertising Services (At Last) - On A $31 Billion Run Rate". Advertising services brought in $9.7 billion in the fourth quarter of 2021, up by about a third, and $31.2 billion for the year, about 7% of Amazon's revenue. What remained in "other" was worth about $710 million in the quarter. "It got to the point where it was a size that we felt we needed to break it out," Olsavsky said. He also offered a line that reads differently in 2026 than it did then: "Longer term, the Amazon DSP opportunity is something we'll continue to work and refine." CNBC, reporting the same disclosure, compared it with Microsoft's advertising revenue, which Satya Nadella had said exceeded $10 billion in 2021, and with total 2021 revenue of $4.12 billion at Snap and $2.58 billion at Pinterest. Amazon's advertising business was already larger than all three put together.

The pandemic arrived at Amazon as a logistics crisis before it became an advertising windfall. On March 17, 2020, Amazon told sellers it would temporarily prioritise household staples, medical supplies and other high-demand products at its fulfilment centres in the United States and Europe, which meant that many brands paying for Sponsored Products placements could not restock the items those placements promoted. The same day, Bloomberg reported that Amazon had cut its own spending on Google advertising, pulling back from Shopping ads at the moment when demand for its goods was outrunning its ability to deliver them. For a few weeks the question was not how much advertisers would spend on Amazon, but whether there was anything to advertise.

The answer came quickly. Digiday's Seb Joseph reported on May 1, 2020 that Amazon's advertising business had grown 44% in the first quarter to $3.91 billion, against 13% growth to $28 billion at Google and 17% growth to $17.4 billion at Facebook. Merkle's client data showed Sponsored Products sales up 70% year on year and Sponsored Brands sales up 131%, on a 118% increase in cost. Tinuiti, tracking about $400 million of US spend, saw Sponsored Products ad growth slow to 6% in the last week of March as stock ran out, before recovering. Danielle Waller of Merkle described what was happening to budgets: "we're seeing advertisers take money from their holistic budgets to support Amazon as a growth channel."

The second quarter made the shift structural. Amazon's revenue rose 40% to $88.9 billion, and the "other" line, which Marketing Dive described as mostly advertising, grew 41% to $4.22 billion. Amazon itself, Olsavsky told analysts, had cut its own marketing spend by roughly a third in the quarter because it did not need to stimulate demand it could barely fulfil. AdNews in Australia quoted eMarketer's Andrew Lipsman: "Amazon has strengthened its future position in key growth areas like grocery, health and advertising." Prime Day, normally a July event, was moved to October 13 and 14 that year, pushing one of the heaviest advertising weeks of the calendar into the fourth quarter.

By the end of 2020, the line had grown between 41% and 49% in every quarter since the third quarter of 2019, and in the fourth quarter it jumped 64% to $7.95 billion, overtaking subscription services, GeekWire reported. Olsavsky credited the move of Prime Day into the quarter, and said: "I would say that there's been a recovery in advertising spend as the year progressed." Michael Pachter of Wedbush was less impressed by the surprise than by the arithmetic: "It's not really surprising in the context of their sales growth." Across the whole year the line reached about $21.5 billion, roughly half as much again as in 2019.

What the pandemic did to Amazon's advertising business was to move a large share of everyday shopping, for groceries, household goods and pharmacy items as well as electronics, onto a site where every search results page carried sponsored placements. Brands that had treated Amazon as a distribution channel learned to treat it as a media channel, because the product listing was now the shop window. Agencies built retail media practices around it. Amazon, in turn, learned that advertising revenue tracked retail traffic closely and that the two could be grown together. That lesson informed everything it did next.

The first full year with a published advertising number was also the last of the pandemic boom. Advertising services reached $31.2 billion in 2021, with growth of 32% in the fourth quarter. Then retail growth stalled. Marketplace Pulse reported on February 3, 2023 that Amazon's first-party retail sales had fallen 0.9% to $220 billion in 2022, while its advertising business expanded by 21%. Juozas Kaziukenas summed up the year: "Amazon's growth in 2022 was nearly flat." Advertising kept growing anyway, which was the point. Adweek reported on February 2, 2023 that Amazon's ad business continued to surge even as Google and Meta faced slowdowns, with fourth-quarter advertising sales of $11.6 billion, up 19%. Forrester calculated that the $38 billion from advertising services in 2022 was nearly double the level of two years earlier.

In 2023 growth picked up again. Marketing Dive's headline on February 2, 2024 was "Amazon's Q4 ad sales total $14.6B as Prime Video ads begin", and the quarter's 27% rise owed nothing to video: Olsavsky said that "the strength in advertising was primarily driven by sponsored products." The full year came to $46.9 billion. The following year, 2024, was the first above $50 billion: Adweek reported on February 6, 2025 that Amazon's ad revenue was $56.2 billion, with $17.3 billion in the fourth quarter, up 18%. That was also the year Prime Video began to matter. Digiday's Seb Joseph and Krystal Scanlon reported on February 20, 2025 that, in one agency sample, the demand-side platform's share of Prime Video ad spend rose from 26% in the third quarter of 2024 to 36% in the fourth, and that Tinuiti's clients spent more than eight times as much on Prime Video in the fourth quarter as in the first.
In 2025, advertising revenue reached $68.6 billion. The quarterly figures since then show both the momentum and the first real interruption to it.

The third quarter of 2026 is the anomaly in that table, and it deserves attention because it is the closest thing to a counter-signal in Amazon's advertising record. PPC Land reported on October 29 that advertising revenue rose only 10.9% to $19.64 billion, down $172 million from the second quarter. Amazon attributed the slowdown to "timing anomalies primarily related to Prime Day (and a couple other timing factors)". Prime Day ran from June 23 to 26 in the United States, inside the second quarter, where it had previously fallen in July. Olsavsky said that "Prime Day timing shifted this year, with the event occurring in Q2 for most large countries." AdExchanger's Joanna Gerber reported that Andy Jassy also pointed to the absence of NBA games in the quarter. The combined second and third quarters came to $39.45 billion, up 18.1%, which is a fairer measure of the underlying rate. For the fourth quarter, Amazon said: "We expect year-over-year advertising revenue to grow in the high teens in fourth quarter 2026." Digiday's Ronan Shields noted that Amazon expects total fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion.

One explanation Amazon rejected is that AI shopping agents run by other companies are already eating into sponsored search. Adweek reported on October 30, 2026 that Amazon says external AI agents are not hurting its ad business, and quoted Jassy: "Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet." Adweek put Amazon's trailing twelve-month advertising revenue at $78 billion, the same figure PPC Land calculated. There was also a smaller warning sign from the advertising side of the calendar shift. CommerceIQ data reported by PPC Land showed that measured US Prime Day advertising spend fell 8.8% while conversion rose 17.1%, which describes fewer and better-qualified impressions, but also an event at which brands spent less than the year before.
Where Amazon sits in the market

Amazon's advertising revenue is now large enough to be measured against the two companies that have dominated digital advertising for two decades, and the comparison shows a business that is smaller but gaining. Ronan Shields' Ad Tech Briefing for Digiday on September 15, 2026 carried Madison and Wall's estimates of US advertising revenue shares in 2024 and 2025:
Source: Madison and Wall estimates, via Digiday, September 15, 2026.

Luke Stillman of Madison and Wall told Digiday that the three companies are "just going to outperform the average every year", because more spending produces better optimisation data and better optimisation attracts more spending. Globally, WARC's forecast, cited in Sam Bradley's Media Buying Briefing for Digiday on October 12, 2026, has advertising spend growing 11.9% to $1.34 trillion this year, with Alphabet, Amazon and Meta taking 59.7%, about $659.6 billion. Amazon is the smallest of the three, but it is the only one that also sells most of the products being advertised, operates the store in which they are bought and can see the purchase. That is the asset everything else in this story is built on.
Prime Video: the audience Amazon switched on

If there is one decision that explains how Amazon went from a search advertising business to a television advertising business, it was taken in September 2023 and carried out on January 29, 2024. On September 22, 2023, Amazon announced that films and series on Prime Video would carry "limited advertisements" from early 2024, starting in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Canada, with France, Italy, Spain, Mexico and Australia to follow later that year. Members who wanted to avoid them would pay an extra $2.99 a month in the United States. Advanced Television quoted the company's promise that it aimed "to have meaningfully fewer ads than linear TV and other streaming TV providers".

What made the move different from every other streaming service's ad tier was the direction of the default. Netflix and Disney+ had launched cheaper plans with advertising and invited subscribers to move down to them. Amazon put every existing Prime Video member onto the advertising plan at once and asked those who objected to pay to leave it. 9to5Google reported on December 26, 2023 that Amazon had begun emailing members to say that ads would start on January 29, 2024, and that no action was required to keep watching with them. Nobody had to sign up. The largest ad-supported streaming audience in the United States was created by a setting.

Amazon presented the result at its first upfront, in New York on May 14, 2024. Its own recap claimed "an average monthly ad-supported reach of 200 million global customers, 115 million of whom are in the U.S." Paul Kotas, senior vice president of Amazon Ads, framed the pitch around scale: "It's about delivering relevant advertising in Prime Video to over 200 million customers." Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, went further: "No other streaming service can reach the number of customers with premium entertainment that we can." The same event introduced three interactive formats, a shoppable carousel, an interactive pause ad and interactive brand trivia, and announced that Prime Video would carry five NASCAR Cup Series races in 2025. Amazon also claimed a streaming television audience of more than 175 million a month and weekly Thursday Night Football audiences of more than 10 million.

A year later, the US figure had grown again. The Hollywood Reporter reported in May 2025 that Prime Video's US ad-supported reach had reached 130 million. By the fourth quarter of 2025, Amazon said the average ad-supported audience was 315 million viewers across 16 countries, PPC Land reported on February 7, 2026, a little over half as large again as the global figure it had claimed in 2024.

The promise of "meaningfully fewer ads" was kept in the sense that Prime Video still carries much less advertising than broadcast television. It was not kept in the sense that the load stayed where it began. Fortune reported on June 12, 2025, citing an Adweek study, that Prime Video's ad load had risen from two to three and a half minutes an hour to between four and six minutes, against 13 to 16 minutes on linear television. Amazon's reply was that it remained "focused on prioritizing ad innovation over volume." That is roughly a doubling in about 16 months.

The price of leaving the ad tier went up too. PPC Land reported on March 15, 2026 that the US ad-free add-on would rise from $2.99 to $4.99 a month from April 10, 2026, an increase of 67%, under a new name, Prime Video Ultra, with an annual option at $45.99. The full Prime membership costs $14.99 a month or $139 a year, and a standalone Prime Video subscription $8.99. "Delivering ad-free streaming with premium features requires significant investment," Amazon said. PPC Land noted that a US class action over the original switch had been dismissed in July 2025, with the court treating the introduction of ads as a "benefit modification" that Prime's terms permitted.

Germany was less accommodating. On December 19, 2025, the Munich Regional Court ruled in a case brought by the Federation of German Consumer Organisations, the vzbv, that Amazon's February 2024 email telling German members that ads would appear unless they paid EUR 2.99 a month was misleading, and ordered the company to send a correction letter. The judgment was not legally binding at the time it was reported. It remains the clearest legal challenge to the method by which Amazon built its streaming audience: a contract that existing customers had signed without advertising, changed to one with advertising, with the cost of opting out set by Amazon.

A television screen that knows what was bought

The formats Amazon has built for Prime Video are designed to do something conventional television advertising cannot: connect the screen to the shopping basket. The shoppable carousel and interactive pause ads shown at the 2024 upfront allowed a viewer to add a product to an Amazon cart with a remote control. On October 31, 2025, Amazon announced zip-code-level targeting for Prime Video ads, which lets an advertiser generate thousands of local variants from one creative, available through managed and self-service buying in the DSP in the United States. PPC Land's account of the launch, published on November 12, 2025, noted that Prime Video's German reach alone was more than 17 million a month.

Six months later, on May 11, 2026, Amazon introduced Dynamic TV Creative for selected US advertisers in packaged goods, fashion and electronics, with an expansion to live sports and Prime Video Channels planned for the third quarter of 2026. The format assembles a television advertisement from components based on what Amazon knows about the household, and carries calls to action such as "Add to Cart" and "Send to Phone". PPC Land cited an IVA study of 14,518 campaigns from 9,960 advertisers in support of the approach, and quoted Rousseau, a director at CreativeX: "This moves away from a one-size-fits-all approach."

Measurement followed the inventory. In the United Kingdom, the audience measurement body Barb launched its Ads Hub on January 27, 2026 with a Prime Video integration under way, a step that matters because British television budgets are traded on Barb's currency. In the United States, Amazon's argument has been that it does not need a third party to tell it what happened, because it can see the purchase. Alan Moss, Amazon's vice president of global advertising sales, put it most directly in an interview reported by PPC Land on May 14, 2026: "Amazon's not guessing, we're knowing."

Prime Video also became the place where Amazon's demand-side platform found its most compelling inventory. Digiday's Seb Joseph and Krystal Scanlon reported on February 20, 2025 that, in one agency's data, the DSP accounted for 32% of Amazon ad spend in the fourth quarter of 2024, and that its share of Prime Video spend had risen from 26% to 36% in a single quarter. Clare Hogan of Pacvue told Digiday: "Amazon has removed the barrier of entry to the DSP." Shray Joshi of Good Peeps offered a measure of where it sat in the budget: "Amazon DSP for our brands is typically 10-15% of spend once they have maximized sponsored search spend." Prime Video, in other words, was the reason to log in to the DSP, and the DSP was the route through which the rest of Amazon's video supply would later be sold.

The Emmy deal shows how far the ambition now reaches. Amazon and the Television Academy disclosed on October 6, 2026 a six-year agreement making Prime Video the exclusive worldwide home of the Emmy Awards from the 2027 ceremony, ending a rotation among ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC that had run until the 78th ceremony on September 14, 2026. The awards began in 1949. Prime Video will be the first home outside broadcast television in their history, and the stream will need no subscription. It is the kind of tentpole event that, until very recently, only a broadcast network could sell.

Prime Video gave Amazon a large audience. Live sports gave it an audience that advertisers cannot easily buy anywhere else, that watches in real time and that does not skip. The investment began modestly. In 2017, Amazon took the streaming rights to Thursday Night Football from Twitter, reportedly for about $50 million for ten games. In 2021 it signed an 11-season agreement to become the exclusive home of the package from 2022, at a reported cost of about $1 billion a year. GeekWire reported that the deal would begin a year early and cover 15 regular-season games and one preseason game. Marie Donoghue, then vice president of global sports video, said: "This expedited deal is an immediate differentiator for us as a service."

The first exclusive broadcast, the Kansas City Chiefs against the Los Angeles Chargers on September 15, 2022, averaged 13 million viewers on Nielsen data, against 8.84 million for the NFL Network's Thursday games in 2021. CNBC reported that the median age of the audience was 47, against 53 for the previous broadcasts. Jay Marine, then head of sports at Prime Video, said: "By every measure, Thursday Night Football on Prime Video was a resounding success." Amazon's 2024 upfront materials claimed that the audience had grown 24% in its second season and that viewers were seven years younger than on broadcast.

The growth since then has been steady. PPC Land reported on October 31, 2025 that the 2025 season was averaging 15.3 million viewers, and on February 7, 2026 that the full season had averaged more than 15 million, up 16%, with a Wild Card playoff game between the Green Bay Packers and the Chicago Bears drawing 31.6 million. In 2026, Adweek reported on October 30 that Thursday Night Football, in its fifth season on Prime Video, was averaging 17.7 million viewers, up 17%. Adweek's Bill Bradley reported on October 24 on how Amazon made a stronger partnership play in Thursday Night Football in year 5: the number of advertisers rose 6% on the year, and 17% of the season's advertisers were new both to the broadcast and to Prime Video. Amy McDevitt, who leads live sports sales partnerships, was pushing sponsors to buy across Amazon's other businesses as well.

Basketball followed. In July 2024, Amazon agreed an 11-year deal with the National Basketball Association from the 2025-26 season, covering 66 regular-season games a year and playoff rounds, along with WNBA games through 2036. GeekWire, citing Bloomberg, put the cost at about $1.8 billion a year. Adam Silver, the league's commissioner, said that "the digital opportunities with Amazon align perfectly with the global interest in the NBA." The first regular-season game on Prime Video drew 1.25 million US viewers in October 2025. By the end of the first season, Amazon reported a peak of 6.5 million US viewers, and play-in games had drawn more than 3 million.

The deals have produced exactly what Amazon's advertising team wanted from them: new buyers. In the PPC Land interview published on May 14, 2026, Moss said that Thursday Night Football had brought in 80 net new advertisers and the NBA 30 in its first year. Moss joined Amazon in July 2020 and had the football deal done within nine months. He rejected the idea that Amazon's streaming and retail advertising are separate propositions: "I don't think of those as separate worlds." Asked whether AI agents would ever handle upfront negotiations, he answered with one word: "Never."

By the second quarter of 2026, there was nothing left to sell. Andy Jassy told analysts in late July that inventory on Thursday Night Football, NBA, WNBA and NASCAR had all sold out. The third quarter then showed the other side of a sports-driven business. With no NBA games between the end of the finals and the season opener on October 23, Jassy cited the absence of basketball as one of the reasons advertising growth slowed to 10.9%. Live sports supply is lumpy, and an advertising business that relies on it inherits its calendar.

Amazon is also building technology into the broadcasts. On October 28, 2026 it published a technical account of Prime 360, an AI system that generates new replay frames in selected NBA broadcasts, and said that running its diffusion models on Amazon's own Trainium chips cut processing latency by more than 40%, without giving a baseline. Amazon did not say whether the replays carry sponsorship.

Taken together, the two league agreements commit Amazon to roughly $2.8 billion a year in sports rights on the reported figures, which on Landline's arithmetic is a little under 4% of its advertising revenue over the twelve months to September 2026. That proportion is low by the standards of any broadcaster, and it is the reason Amazon can treat sports as a customer acquisition cost for its wider advertising business rather than as a programme that must pay for itself. Moss's 80 and 30 net new advertisers are the return Amazon talks about. The Prime memberships those games help to retain, and the products those advertisers then sell on Amazon, are the return it does not have to.
Building the cheapest DSP in the market

Amazon's demand-side platform is older than its streaming business. Amazon sold display advertising through a buying tool it called the Amazon Advertising Platform for years before the 2018 rename, and by October 2017 Digiday was reporting that buyers considered the technology good enough for Amazon's DSP to become a rival to Google, with fees already described as among the lowest in the market. For most of the period since, the DSP's main selling point was not its interface, which buyers often criticised, but two things no other platform could offer: Amazon's shopper audiences, and a price that undercut everyone else.

The price story is the most consistent part of Amazon's pitch, and it is also the most frequently misreported. In November 2024, Digiday wrote that advertisers typically paid 10% of intended spend through the DSP, against 15% for Google and 20% for The Trade Desk, although the managed service option demanded a minimum of $50,000. Amazon's own documentation, summarised by PPC Land on July 18, 2025 when it launched an ad tech activation partners programme, set the fully managed option at a $50,000 minimum, a 15% service fee and a 10% DSP platform fee.

Then the headline rates fell further. In April 2025, a beta tester told AdExchanger that programmatic guaranteed deals carried 0% DSP fees on Amazon media and 1% on a set of streaming publishers, with Amazon Marketing Cloud and data fees reducing the total savings, while The Trade Desk's take rate had run between 19% and 21% since 2017. Amazon's pitch deck, seen by Digiday in May 2025, "touts a 1% tech fee for programmatic guaranteed deals on premium open web inventory." Digiday also described Amazon courting buyers with loss-leader tactics, including an extra 10% of a new advertiser's video buy, capped at $250,000.

By October 2025, buyers told Digiday that Amazon's DSP fees typically ranged between 4% and 8%, sometimes falling to 1% and occasionally disappearing. Adweek reported on October 24, 2025 that Amazon had offered at least one agency a free head-to-head test against a rival DSP, covering inventory, technology and measurement costs. PPC Land's summary of the December 3, 2025 platform consolidation recorded no fee on programmatic guaranteed deals for Amazon-owned media and 1% on the open web.

Those numbers need to be read with care, because the 1% figure that buyers repeat has a narrower scope than it is often given. Both the zero and the 1% describe programmatic guaranteed deals, one way of buying on the platform, not the rate on everything that runs through it. Data targeting and audience fees are charged on top. When Amazon explained how its regulatory advertising fees are calculated, PPC Land reported in August 2024, it described DSP campaign costs as comprising media cost, audience fees and platform fees. Those regulatory advertising fees, it should be said, pass on digital services taxes, and are not a platform fee at all. Inside Amazon Marketing Cloud, third-party signals sit behind a subscription tier called Paid Features, and Amazon has made its own paid audience and retail purchase features free to query only until the end of 2026, without saying what they will cost from January 1, 2027.

The table carries one entry that cuts against the rest. In May 2026, an agency executive told Digiday that minimums for direct DSP access had been pushed into the "tens of millions", in Digiday's coverage of that month's upfronts. A platform that charges almost nothing on its own inventory but requires very large commitments for direct access is a platform that wants large buyers in its own interface and everyone else in its simplified products or dealing through resellers. DVA+, with no minimum spend, is the simplified product. That distinction matters for what comes later in this story.
Why low fees are affordable for Amazon

Vlad Chubakov, associate director of programmatic at Delve Deeper, put the logic in one sentence to PPC Land in August 2026: "Amazon can slash margins because they own the pipes." A standalone DSP such as The Trade Desk earns its revenue from the fee it takes on media it does not own. Amazon earns its revenue from the media itself, from the audience data advertisers buy to target it, from the measurement products it sells to evaluate it and, increasingly, from the cloud contracts that sit underneath. A low platform fee, and none at all on Amazon's own guaranteed inventory, costs Amazon little when every dollar of Prime Video or Thursday Night Football bought through the DSP is a dollar of Amazon advertising revenue in any case.

There is a cost to the advertiser that the headline rate does not show, and the comparison with Meta makes it visible. Meta has never charged advertisers a platform fee; its take is the auction itself. A buyer on Meta pays nothing for the software and everything through the clearing price. Amazon is moving towards the same model from the other direction: as more of what runs through its buying tool is Amazon's own inventory, priced by Amazon's own auctions or guaranteed deals, the platform fee becomes less relevant to what Amazon earns, and the price of the media becomes more so. Sarah Caputo, founder of the buy-side consultancy Fraction Method, found in an AdExchanger column on September 9, 2026 that Amazon's documentation describes its invitation-only Private Auction product, including Prime Video inventory, as clearing at a "variable CPM based on optimization," with no buyer-visible floor or clearing formula. "Platforms built the systems, and only platforms can fully explain how they set the price," she wrote.
Buying the pipes: the supply deals of 2025 and 2026

A cheap DSP needs something to buy. From the middle of 2025, Amazon set about connecting its buying platform to almost every large source of premium video and audio supply in the United States and many beyond it. Digiday later described the result as an eighteen-month run of supply acquisitions, in which Amazon did not build the audience but bought the pipe to it and then undercut rivals on fees.

The first and largest was Roku. On June 16, 2025, Amazon and Roku announced what they called the largest authenticated connected television partnership, reaching 80 million US connected TV households, more than 80% of the total. Amazon claimed advertisers could reach 40% more unique viewers with the same budget while cutting frequency by nearly 30%. "Our exclusive partnership with Roku is a giant leap for advertisers," Kotas said. A day later, on June 17, Disney said its inventory across Disney+, Hulu and ESPN would become available in the DSP through its DRAX programmatic platform, for all DSP advertisers from the third quarter of 2025, with Disney+ inventory in eight European markets as well. Amazon said its DSP now reached 275 million monthly US ad-supported customers. Kelly MacLean, vice president of Amazon DSP, called it "a significant leap forward in advertising effectiveness."

Netflix followed on September 10, 2025, when Amazon announced that Netflix inventory would be buyable through the DSP in 11 markets from the fourth quarter of 2025: the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Mexico, Canada, Japan, Brazil, Italy, Germany and Australia. Kotas said that the goal was to "remove the guesswork for advertisers by making it simple to manage all of their TV planning and buying with Amazon Ads." Audio arrived within weeks. SiriusXM Media, with 160 million monthly digital listeners across SiriusXM, Pandora and SoundCloud through AdsWizz, integrated with the DSP on September 16, and Spotify's global audio and video inventory followed in early October, giving access to 696 million monthly listeners in nine markets on Amazon's later count.

The most symbolic addition came from Microsoft. When Microsoft decided to wind down its Invest DSP by February 28, 2026, PPC News Feed reported on October 12, 2025 that Amazon DSP would be the preferred partner for Microsoft's advertisers, with Microsoft Monetize joining the Amazon Certified Supply Exchange through a preferred-partner integration. A company that had spent two decades trying to build its own display advertising business handed its buyers to Amazon.

The pattern continued through 2026. Triton Digital, the audio technology company owned by iHeartMedia, added Amazon DSP as a demand partner across more than 80 countries on July 15. On September 10, AWS Elemental added yield optimisation that fills unsold live ad breaks with Amazon Ads demand for streaming publishers using Amazon Publisher Services, and Amazon Ads and OpenAI opened a pilot that lets select US advertisers extend DSP campaigns into ChatGPT, with Delta Vacations the first to test it. On October 6, Sky Media made its UK and Irish streaming inventory buyable through Amazon Ads Agent, across Sky Go, NOW, Sky Glass, Sky Q and Sky Stream, with programmatic guaranteed deals available immediately. In late October, PPC Land reported that Pinterest sells ads through Amazon and Google DSPs in three regions, not Europe, with Amazon Ads DVA+ named among the buying platforms. And in early November, Adweek reported that Amazon advertisers can now target shoppers that buy elsewhere, through an integration between the data company Attain and DVA+ that uses purchase behaviour at Walmart, Dollar General, Kroger, Walgreens and Sephora.
